Chapter 3: The Dilemma of Divine Approval—Is Goodness Chosen or Commanded?
Picture this: the conversation takes a sharp turn, and suddenly, a profound question pops up.
If piety means doing what the gods love, then here's the real puzzle— is something good just because the gods approve of it, or do the gods approve of it because it’s already good?
At first glance, it might sound simple, right? But this question goes straight to the core of how we think about morality and who gets to decide what’s right.
Imagine someone who’s always trying to do what’s right, convinced that following rules set by a higher power is the safest bet. Now, what happens if those rules can change, or if the higher power disagrees? That idea alone can shake your confidence. If goodness is based only on divine approval, then what’s good and bad could shift on a whim—totally arbitrary, depending on who’s in charge. But if the gods love what’s good because it’s good, then there must be a standard of right and wrong that exists, no matter what anyone—gods included—thinks.
The older man, never satisfied with easy answers, pushed this dilemma even further. He asked the younger to think about whether the gods’ love actually makes something holy, or if holiness is something that stands on its own, no matter how the gods feel about it.
The younger man, caught completely off guard, struggled to find a clear answer. If he said the gods’ love creates holiness, then literally anything could become holy—just because the gods decided to love it. But if he claimed the gods love what’s already holy, then holiness must have a life of its own, separate from any divine command.
This back-and-forth forced both men to face the limits of what they knew. It became obvious that simply leaning on tradition or authority wouldn’t solve the problem. The older man’s way—asking sharp, simple questions, and refusing to settle for half-answers—quickly uncovered just how complicated our beliefs really are.
Let’s be honest—most of us, when faced with these kinds of dilemmas, feel uncomfortable. It’s so much easier to trust the wisdom that’s been handed down to us, to believe that the old rules are enough. But this conversation, right outside the courthouse, made it clear that truly understanding what’s right means more than just obeying. It means being willing to question even the things we hold most sacred.
The younger man, who started out so sure of his duty, suddenly found himself trapped between two answers that didn’t satisfy him. If he depended on the gods’ approval, morality could become nothing more than the mood of the moment. But if he argued that goodness exists on its own, he was left with a whole new puzzle—where does that standard come from?
The older man, for his part, seemed less interested in giving solutions than in showing just how tricky the question really is.
In that moment, their talk became much more than a debate about piety. It turned into a meditation on what morality means, how authority shapes us, and how tough it can be to find firm ground in a world that often feels uncertain.
This dilemma isn’t just ancient history—it’s still something that troubles anyone who’s ever tried to figure out the balance between faith and reason, between following tradition and searching for truth.
Through their honest exchange, one thing became clear: finding what’s truly right takes more than following orders. It takes a willingness to look deep within, to ask the hard questions—even when the answers aren’t easy. Those unsettling questions? They’re actually an invitation to a deeper kind of understanding, one that respects the world’s complexity and reminds us just how much we still have to learn.
